title: Pardons
lead: The power to pardon under ==Arts 72 and 161== is one of the Republic's most potent symbols of humanism — where justice is not merely cold and legalistic but tempered with compassion. It embodies a paradox: it allows an ==unelected figurehead to override solemn judicial verdicts==.

head: Case
Holding
rows: Pardon power ==cannot override due process==; must be reasoned.
==Not personal discretion== — President/Governor must act on ==CoM advice==.
Power is broad, includes ==revisiting the merits==; not judicial in nature but subject to ==limited review==.
Must consider ==post-conviction behaviour==; its absence can invalidate the pardon.
==Undue delay== in deciding mercy petitions can ground ==commutation of a death sentence==.

head: Country
Framework
rows: Art II, Sec 2 — pardons except in impeachment; limited judicial review ([[Hoffa v. Saxbe]]).
Mercy by the Crown on the ==Home Secretary's advice==; review limited ([[R v. Secretary of State, ex parte Bentley]]).
Art 45 — ==unfettered== presidential power; not subject to judicial review.
Art 49 — vests in the President, exercised only on ==PM's advice==.

blocks.text: The challenge lies not in curtailing the power, but in disciplining its exercise — with procedural fairness, timely action, and judicious restraint. For in a nation where the rule of law reigns supreme, even mercy must march to the rhythm of reason.
